title: Why is AriZona Iced Tea still 99 cents?
question: Why does a giant can of AriZona Iced Tea still cost 99 cents?
description: AriZona's 23-ounce can cost 99 cents in 1992 and still does. The company spends little on advertising, cut its costs (thinner cans, deliveries at night), and is family owned with no debt, so it sells more cans instead of charging more per can. The twist: the price is printed on the can, yet some stores charge more anyway.

scenes.narration: Why does this giant can of iced tea still cost 99 cents? It cost 99 cents in 1992, too.
Thirty years of rising prices, and its price line stays flat.
Reason one: almost no ads. Other drink giants pay millions for TV commercials. AriZona mostly lets word of mouth do the selling.
Reason two: it got cheaper to make. The cans got thinner, and trucks deliver at night to skip the traffic.
Reason three: no one to pay back. A family owns it, with no debt, so it can sell more cans instead of charging more per can.
But here's the twist. The 99 cents is printed right on the can. Still, some stores charge more anyway.

claims.claim: The 23-ounce can cost 99 cents in 1992 and still does.
The price stayed at 99 cents for 30 years (1992-2022) while prices in general rose.
AriZona relies on word of mouth rather than big advertising campaigns, while other drink brands spend millions on ads (a 30-second Super Bowl ad is about $6.5 million).
The cans were made thinner (about 40% less aluminum) to hold costs down.
Trucks deliver at night / overnight to avoid daytime traffic.
The company is family owned (Don Vultaggio and his sons) and debt-free.
It offsets rising costs by selling more cans (volume) rather than raising the price.
The 99-cent price is printed on the can.
Some stores charge more than 99 cents anyway ($1.59 and up, some up to $2).
